note: Every measure below is count-free: it does not require knowing which vertebra is which. Level names cannot be assigned from a spine-limited field of view, because the same bone is called a sacralised L5 or a lumbarised S1 depending only on where the count starts.

panels.section_note: Every case comes from CT colonography -- a colorectal cancer SCREENING examination. The age floor visible in the data is the screening guideline showing through, not a choice made here. So this is an asymptomatic screening population rather than a surgical or back-pain series: the spinopelvic measures below sit closer to a reference range than a clinical cohort would, and the transitional variants were found incidentally.
panels.title: Age, by sex
panels.subtitle: a screening population: the lower bound is the guideline, not a filter
panels.caption: Median 58 years in women and 59 in men. Nothing below the screening age threshold appears because nothing below it was scanned.

panels.title: Sex
panels.subtitle: as recorded in the source metadata
panels.caption: Recorded in the source collection, not inferred from the images. Cases with no recorded value are shown rather than dropped.

panels.title: How each record was assembled
panels.subtitle: spine and pelvic labels do not always land on the same acquisition
panels.caption: Each patient was scanned prone and supine. Where both label sets landed on one acquisition the record is fused; otherwise the two are exported separately, which is why a patient can appear as more than one record.

panels.title: Transitional label carried by the source
panels.subtitle: from the source collections, not adjudicated here
panels.xlabel: Transitional label carried by the source
panels.caption: These are the labels the source collections carried. They are shown as they arrived, and are not all expert-adjudicated -- which is exactly why the measures on this page are count-free and do not depend on them.

panels.section_note: Surgeons locate the lumbar spine by feel before they see it, and the iliac crest is the landmark they use. These are the measures where that habit meets the anatomy in this cohort.
panels.title: The iliac crest does not always reach L4
panels.subtitle: the level the crest rises to, by how many rib-free vertebrae there are
panels.xlabel: vertebral level the iliac crest reaches
panels.caption: The crest reaches L4 in 83% of people with a typical rib-free count, and in 4 rib-free 46%, 6 rib-free 62% of those without one. The landmark is least reliable in exactly the patients whose levels are hardest to count, so the two errors compound rather than cancel. Shown as percentages because the groups differ in size by more than twenty to one.

panels.title: The disc above a transitional segment
panels.subtitle: lowest disc gap divided by the disc above it
panels.caption: A transitional segment moves less, and the level above it is described as taking up that motion and degenerating earlier. A narrower disc above raises this ratio. Medians: 5 rib-free (typical) 1.53, 4 rib-free 1.71, 6 rib-free 1.55. Shown as distributions; nothing here is a test.

panels.title: Non-rib-bearing vertebrae
panels.subtitle: counted BETWEEN the lowest rib and the sacrum — an interval, not a level
panels.caption: Five is typical. Four and six are where transitional anatomy sits — and which of the two you see does not tell you what to call it.

panels.title: Lowest rib length, as a fraction of the rib above
panels.subtitle: hypoplastic twelfth ribs form their own population
panels.caption: Two modes, near 0.68 and near 0.32 — not one distribution with a tail. That shape is what a discrete developmental variant looks like. The curve is a kernel density estimate; the ticks beneath it are the cases themselves, thinned.

panels.title: Lowest disc gap ÷ the disc above it
panels.subtitle: dimensionless, so it compares across patients
panels.caption: A rudimentary lowest disc runs low. Values near zero also arise from fusion of any cause — congenital, surgical or bridging osteophyte — which is why this measure alone cannot say why a gap closed.

panels.title: How far the lowest lumbar reaches, and how close it comes to the ala
panels.subtitle: one point per side — the asymmetry is the phenotype
panels.caption: Castellvi grades on a process that approaches, articulates with, or fuses to the sacral ala. Span and gap carry most of that without naming the level.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Pelvic incidence
panels.subtitle: position-independent: identical standing, seated and supine
panels.caption: A morphological property of the pelvis rather than a posture, which is why a supine CT can be compared to a standing reference without apology. Measured median 54.7 against Vialle's 54.7 +- 10.6 in 260 asymptomatic adults -- agreement to a decimal place, on the measure whose definition is least ambiguous.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Sacral slope
panels.subtitle: postural: the reference is standing, this cohort is supine
panels.caption: The sacral plate against the horizontal. Measured 36.9 against a standing reference of 41.0 +- 8.4. Lying down rotates the pelvis and lowers the slope, so sitting below a standing reference is the expected direction rather than a discrepancy.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Pelvic tilt
panels.subtitle: postural, reported supine
panels.caption: Pelvic incidence less sacral slope; it rises as a pelvis retroverts to compensate for lost lordosis. Measured 13.9 against 13 +- 6.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Lumbar lordosis, supine
panels.subtitle: no single published reference -- the number depends on which arc is measured
panels.caption: Measured here from the superior endplate of the topmost lumbar vertebra to the superior endplate of S1, supine, and only where the arc reaches L1. Published means range from about 43 to 60 degrees depending on whether the arc is L1-S1, L1-L5 or T12-S1, so no single line is drawn: choosing one would be choosing a number to agree with. Supine also sits about 4.6 degrees below standing.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: PI-LL mismatch
panels.subtitle: the decision-maker: beyond about 10 degrees predicts residual pain after fusion
panels.caption: Centred near zero across an unoperated cohort, which is the check that the two angles were measured independently and still agree.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Iliac crest above the L4-5 disc
panels.subtitle: the lateral corridor: positive means the crest obstructs a lateral approach
panels.caption: The dashed line is the published 12 mm cutoff, above which subsidence risk rises after oblique lateral fusion at that level.
panels.xlabel: Iliac crest above the L4-5 disc (mm)

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Lowest rib to iliac crest
panels.subtitle: the other boundary of the same corridor
panels.caption: This is where the rib work becomes operative: a hypoplastic or absent twelfth rib moves the upper limit of the working window.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Narrowest lumbar pedicle
panels.subtitle: selects screw diameter, and is itself a phenotype
panels.caption: Measured at the isthmus, per side, taking the narrower of the two.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Does the lumbar spine match the pelvis it sits on?
panels.subtitle: one point per case; the diagonal is a perfect match
panels.caption: Points below the diagonal have less lordosis than their pelvis calls for. The cloud sits ON the line, which is what an unoperated cohort should do and is the strongest evidence these two angles were measured independently.

panels.section: Spinopelvic alignment and the surgical corridor
panels.title: Pelvic incidence by sex
panels.subtitle: reported because the cohort carries age and sex, not because it separates
panels.caption: Median 55.1 degrees in women against 54.7 in men, a difference of 0.4. Pelvic dimorphism is strong in shape -- subpubic angle, inlet proportions, the sciatic notch -- and pelvic incidence is not one of those measures, so a null here agrees with the series that report no sex difference in it.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.section_note: Adult spinal deformity is usually described in patients who already have it. These are people who came in for a colon screening, so what follows is the same mechanism seen before anyone complained of anything.
panels.title: Pelvic incidence holds still while the spine compensates around it
panels.subtitle: median and interquartile range, by decade
panels.caption: Pelvic incidence is a morphological property of the pelvis, fixed once the sacroiliac joints mature, and it moves -2.4 degrees across these decades. That flatness is a negative control: a cohort cannot fake it. Everything around it moves -- the pelvis retroverts, lordosis is lost, and the sacral slope follows because it is pelvic incidence less tilt. The lordosis a spine NEEDS is set by a number that never changes; what it HAS declines.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.title: The gap between the lordosis a spine needs and the lordosis it has
panels.subtitle: PI-LL mismatch, median and interquartile range, by decade
panels.caption: Median 2.3 degrees in the youngest decade here and 7.8 in the oldest, against a threshold near 10 beyond which residual pain after fusion becomes likely -- most of the widening comes from the pelvis retroverting rather than from lordosis collapsing. This is the same quantity surgeons plan a correction around, measured in people who were not being assessed for anything spinal.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.title: Pelvic tilt, by age and sex
panels.subtitle: median and interquartile range, women against men
panels.caption: The two bands sit on top of each other: the median difference between women and men across these decades is 1.2 degrees, on a measure whose interquartile range is several times that. Pelvic SHAPE is strongly dimorphic in this same cohort -- see the relative width panels -- but how the spine sits on that pelvis is not. Shape answers to obstetric constraint; alignment answers to balance, and balance does not care which pelvis it is on.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.title: Lumbar lordosis, by age and sex
panels.subtitle: median and interquartile range, women against men
panels.caption: The two bands sit on top of each other: the median difference between women and men across these decades is 3.2 degrees, on a measure whose interquartile range is several times that. Pelvic SHAPE is strongly dimorphic in this same cohort -- see the relative width panels -- but how the spine sits on that pelvis is not. Shape answers to obstetric constraint; alignment answers to balance, and balance does not care which pelvis it is on.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.title: Pelvic incidence does not move
panels.subtitle: one distribution per decade; the tick on each is its median
panels.caption: Every decade sits on the same reference band. Pelvic incidence is fixed once the sacroiliac joints mature, so this is the negative control for the two panels beside it -- a cohort cannot fake a distribution that refuses to move.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.title: Pelvic tilt climbs
panels.subtitle: one distribution per decade; the tick on each is its median
panels.caption: The whole distribution walks to the right and its upper tail lengthens. A pelvis retroverts to hold the trunk upright as lordosis is lost, and the cases doing the most of it are the ones in that growing tail.

panels.section: What changes with age, and what does not
panels.title: Lumbar lordosis, largely held
panels.subtitle: one distribution per decade; the tick on each is its median
panels.caption: Medians of 52.2, 53.4, 52.9 and 51.8 degrees across the decades: this cohort does not lose much lordosis at all. That is worth saying plainly rather than dressing up, and it fits who these people are -- an asymptomatic screening population, not a deformity clinic. The pelvis beside it retroverts anyway, which is the more sensitive early sign. No reference line is drawn: published means run from 43 to 60 degrees depending on which arc is measured, so any single line would be one chosen to agree with.

panels.title: Bone density by decade, women
panels.subtitle: L1 trabecular attenuation, one distribution per decade
panels.caption: Median 174 HU in the first decade shown falling to 132 in the last. The median is the least of it: what matters clinically is the low tail crossing the 110 HU line, because that is where the fractures come from, and a median with an error bar cannot show a tail thickening.

panels.title: Bone density by decade, men
panels.subtitle: L1 trabecular attenuation, one distribution per decade
panels.caption: Median 168 HU in the first decade shown falling to 143 in the last. The median is the least of it: what matters clinically is the low tail crossing the 110 HU line, because that is where the fractures come from, and a median with an error bar cannot show a tail thickening.

panels.title: Pelvic width, across the iliac crests
panels.subtitle: the widest span of the bony pelvis
panels.xlabel: Pelvic width, across the iliac crests (mm)
panels.caption: The measurement most people mean by pelvic width. Men are wider in absolute terms because men are larger overall; the female pelvis is wider relative to its size, and that shows in shape measures rather than in this one. Median 272 mm in women against 283 mm in men, a difference of 10 mm.
panels.section_note: Pelvic incidence -- the angle above -- does not separate by sex, and several published series agree that it does not. Sexual dimorphism in the pelvis is a matter of SHAPE: how wide it is, how round the inlet is, how the sacrum is proportioned. Those are measured here, drawn as two overlaid distributions so the separation is visible rather than asserted, and each caption gives both medians and the gap between them.

panels.title: Width across the hip joints
panels.subtitle: centre to centre between the femoral heads
panels.caption: Measured from the part of the femur in contact with the acetabulum. The femur labels run 61-109 mm from head to shaft, so a whole-label centroid sits down the shaft and read 18 mm too wide before this was corrected. Median 166 mm in women against 167 mm in men, a difference of 2 mm.

panels.title: Pelvic width, relative to skeletal size
panels.subtitle: bi-iliac breadth divided by vertebral body width
panels.xlabel: bi-iliac breadth divided by vertebral body width
panels.caption: In absolute millimetres men are wider, because men are larger. The textbook statement is that the female pelvis is relatively broader, and relatively needs a denominator -- here the mean superior endplate width of L2 to L4, which is a standard skeletal size proxy and is not part of the pelvis. Median 6.52 in women against 5.90 in men, a difference of +0.62 -- the direction the literature describes, and the opposite of what the absolute widths show.

panels.title: Hip joint separation, relative to skeletal size
panels.subtitle: distance between femoral heads divided by vertebral body width
panels.xlabel: distance between femoral heads divided by vertebral body width
panels.caption: The sharper version of the same finding. In absolute terms the hip joints sit almost the same distance apart in both sexes -- 165.5 mm against 167.0 -- while male vertebrae are meaningfully larger. The female pelvis reaches the same span on a smaller frame. Median 3.96 in women against 3.49 in men, a difference of +0.48 -- the direction the literature describes, and the opposite of what the absolute widths show.

panels.section: How the lumbar spine changes as it descends
panels.title: Transverse process span, level by level
panels.subtitle: widest left-right extent of the vertebra, tip to tip
panels.xlabel: tip to tip across the transverse processes (mm)
panels.caption: Measured as the left-right extent of the vertebra at each level. Read with care: against published tip-to-tip figures this runs high, by about 5 mm at L1 and 30 mm at L5, and the published series peak at L3 and fall to L5 where these rise. At the lower levels the extent includes the lateral mass and pars, not the process tip alone, so the level-to-level trend here should not be read as anatomy until the measurement is put on identified landmarks.
panels.section_note: Almost every dimension of a lumbar vertebra grows from L1 downward, because each level carries everything above it. That makes the gradient a stronger check than any single measurement: it either reproduces the published trend or it does not. Two of the four measured here reproduce and are shown; anterior body height and the wedge ratio do not, and are not.

panels.section: How the lumbar spine changes as it descends
panels.title: Vertebral bodies grow taller under load
panels.subtitle: anterior body height, level by level
panels.xlabel: anterior body height, level by level (mm)
panels.caption: Published series run from about 29.9 mm at L1 to 34.5 at L5. Measured at the anterior CORTEX -- the wall -- as the tallest column in the anterior half of a mid-sagittal slab. Two earlier attempts measured the extreme anterior edge instead and read 6 to 12 mm, because the front of a vertebral body is a rounded rim that tapers to nothing. Median 28.8 to 32.0mm across 5 levels.

panels.section: How the lumbar spine changes as it descends
panels.title: The spinal canal widens as it descends
panels.subtitle: transverse diameter, level by level
panels.caption: Published series run from about 22 mm at L1 to 26.5 at L5, and that is the gradient here. The canal keeps widening below the end of the cord, where it carries only the cauda equina. Median 23.9 to 30.0mm across 5 levels.

panels.section: How the lumbar spine changes as it descends
panels.title: Vertebral bodies broaden under load
panels.subtitle: superior endplate, side to side
panels.caption: Published series run from about 41.8 mm at L1 to 50.7 at L5; measured here at 41.4, 42.9, 44.6, 47.8 and 51.8 -- both ends within a millimetre. Each curve carries two humps because it pools both sexes and vertebral size is strongly dimorphic; the panel below separates them. L5 needed a separate fix to get there: the cut that isolates the body follows the anterior wall of the spinal canal, and the L5 transverse processes arise far enough forward to survive it, which read 67.5 mm. Each axial slice is now eroded to snap the isthmus joining process to body, and the largest remaining piece is measured. Median 40.6 to 50.8mm across 5 levels.

panels.section: How the lumbar spine changes as it descends
panels.title: Vertebral body size is strongly dimorphic
panels.subtitle: mean L2-L4 superior endplate width, by sex
panels.caption: Median 41.5 mm in women against 47.7 in men, a difference of 6.1 mm and just over one standard deviation of separation. This is why the pooled distribution above carries two humps: it is a mixture, not a misshapen curve. It is also the sharpest sexual dimorphism in this dataset -- sharper than anything in the pelvis, where a difference only appears after normalising for body size.

panels.section_note: Every scan here was taken to look for colorectal polyps, and every one of them also contains a bone density measurement -- no extra dose, no extra table time. Vertebral trabecular attenuation is the most validated of the opportunistic CT measures, and the technique was established on CT colonography, which is exactly what this cohort is.
panels.title: Vertebral bone density, from a scan taken for something else
panels.subtitle: L1 trabecular attenuation -- the published standard site
panels.caption: The dashed line is 110 HU, over 90% specific for osteoporosis. 75 of 801 cases (9.4%) fall below it. Published series put the population mean near 226 HU under age 30, falling about 2.5 HU per year; at this cohort's median age that predicts roughly 155, measured here at 157. L1 is the site both the original work and the 20,000-adult normative series report, because it is the vertebra most reliably present in both abdominal and thoracic CT -- which is what makes the measure opportunistic. L2 to L4 were measured too and agree within 4 HU, which is a check on the region of interest rather than a separate result: a misplaced ROI would not agree with itself across four independently segmented vertebrae.

panels.title: Women start with denser vertebrae and end with less
panels.subtitle: L1 trabecular attenuation, median and interquartile range, by decade
panels.caption: The lines cross. Women begin at 174 HU against 168 for men and end at 132 against 143 -- a swing of -17 HU in the difference between the sexes across these decades. That is postmenopausal bone loss, drawn as a crossover, in people who were not being assessed for bone.

panels.title: How many fall below the osteoporosis threshold
panels.subtitle: share of each group with L1 attenuation under 110 HU
panels.caption: By the oldest decade shown, 31% of women are below a threshold over 90% specific for osteoporosis, against 10% of men. None of these people were referred for bone assessment; the measurement was already in an image taken for the colon.

panels.section_note: Disc degeneration is the commonest finding on any abdominal CT of an adult and is almost never reported, because the scan was ordered for something else. Both measures here follow criteria someone else defined: disc space narrowing is the oldest radiographic sign of degeneration, and gas inside a disc has no normal variant at all.
panels.title: Disc height, level by level
panels.subtitle: measured at the midline, between the vertebral bodies
panels.caption: Medians L1-2 8.8, L2-3 9.6, L3-4 10.4, L4-5 10.4, L5-S1 9.6 mm, against a published lumbar range of 8 to 12 and a peak at the lower levels. An earlier version of this measurement read 4 to 6 mm because it measured RIM TO RIM: vertebral endplates are concave, so the lowest point of the upper body across a wide column is its rim projecting down into the space. Measuring each column separately and taking the median gives the height a radiologist would read.

panels.title: Gas inside the disc, which has no normal variant
panels.subtitle: vacuum phenomenon by level: voxels below -150 HU in the disc space
panels.caption: Gas sits near -1000 HU where a disc is near +50, so this is one of the least ambiguous measurements in the whole gallery -- and there is no normal variant that puts air inside a disc. 167 of 802 cases (20.8%) have it at one level or more, and it climbs steadily from the top of the lumbar spine to the bottom, which is where the load is.

panels.title: Endplate flare
panels.subtitle: endplate width divided by mid-body width
panels.caption: A healthy vertebral body is slightly waisted -- narrower in the middle than at its endplates -- so this ratio sits just above 1.0. Osteophytes grow at the endplate RIM, which raises it further. The right tail is the geometric form of what a radiologist calls endplate spurring.

panels.title: Vertebral wedging, from the same scan
panels.subtitle: lowest lumbar wedge ratio per case: anterior wall height over posterior
panels.caption: An unfractured body sits near 1.0, and the distribution does. The dashed line is 0.80 -- a 20% height reduction, which Genant's grading calls a mild wedge deformity. 26 of 802 cases (3.2%) have at least one lumbar body below it. A falling anterior wall is what a compression fracture looks like, and low trabecular attenuation is what precedes one -- both are in this image, which was ordered for the colon.

panels.title: Sacral base breadth
panels.subtitle: across both alae at the S1 level
panels.caption: Median 116 mm in women against 118 in men. This measurement had to be rebuilt: the label named 'sacrum' in the scheme is documented as the sacrum BELOW S1, with S1 carved out as its own class, so the first version measured S2 to S5 and produced an index of 0.9 in both sexes.

panels.title: Sacral base breadth, relative to skeletal size
panels.subtitle: sacral base divided by vertebral body width
panels.caption: Median 2.75 in women against 2.48 in men, a difference of +0.27. The same normalisation that flips pelvic width: measured against a body-size proxy that is not itself pelvic, the female sacrum is relatively broader.
